case_facts: tenant eviction dispute in Mumbai without proper notice

analysis.summary: A tenant in Mumbai is facing eviction proceedings allegedly initiated without proper legal notice. The dispute concerns the landlord's compliance with mandatory notice requirements before initiating eviction. The matter likely involves protections available to tenants under Maharashtra-specific rent control legislation.

issues.issue: Validity of eviction without serving proper notice to quit
Tenant's protection against eviction under rent control legislation
Mandatory grounds and procedure required for lawful eviction
Right of tenant to challenge eviction notice as defective or invalid
issues.governing_law: Section 106, Transfer of Property Act 1882; Order 37 CPC

precedents.title: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
precedents.snippet: [DEMO SUMMARY] The Court recognised that the right to livelihood is an integral facet of the right to life. While encroachers can be removed, the procedure must be fair and reasonable, and reasonable notice and an opportunity to be heard must be given before eviction.

precedents.title: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar
precedents.snippet: [DEMO SUMMARY] The Court held that a speedy trial is an essential ingredient of the right to life and liberty under Article 21. Undertrial prisoners detained for periods longer than the maximum sentence for their alleged offence must be released; the State must provide free legal aid.

precedents.title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
precedents.snippet: [DEMO SUMMARY] In the absence of legislation, the Court framed binding guidelines placing a positive duty on employers to provide a safe working environment and effective complaint mechanisms. The decision illustrates judicially-created obligations filling a statutory gap.

precedents.title: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India
precedents.snippet: [DEMO SUMMARY] The Court applied the polluter-pays principle, holding that the financial cost of preventing or remedying damage caused by an activity must be borne by the party responsible for the harm. The principle informs liability and compensation analysis across regulatory disputes.
